data.text/markdown:
EARSHOT demo

EARSHOT is a recurrent neural network model of human speech recognition. It listens to speech in the form of a spectrogram, one 10 ms frame at a time, and at every frame it reports how strongly it believes that each word in its lexicon is currently being said. This notebook walks through the basic steps for working with a pretrained model

1. Data

The spectrograms and model weights are too large for the code repository, so they live in a separate data directory. This demo needs the following files: 
EARSHOT/                      <- the data directory
├── GAMMATONE_64_100/         <- model input: one spectrogram per word and speaker
│   ├── Agnes/
│   │   ├── ABLE_AGNES.pickle
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── ...
│   └── MALD/
│       ├── ABLE_MALD.pickle
│       └── ...
└── Models/
    └── LSTM-192x192x192x192-dw1024to10-RMSProp-1e-3-32-25-s0 OneHot-box MALD-1000-test-64-2-20/
        ├── 4419.hdf5         <- network weights after the last training epoch
        └── log.csv           <- training loss
By default, earshot looks for the data directory at ~/Data/EARSHOT. If you put it somewhere else, either
  • set the EARSHOT_DATA_DIR environment variable before starting marimo, or
  • call earshot.set_data_dir() in the cell below.
Using data in /Users/christian/Data/EARSHOT

2. The model

A Model object is a description of a model: its architecture and how it was trained. It does not contain the network itself yet (we will load that in section 5), but it knows where to find the weights, because the name of the model directory is derived from these parameters.
Parameter Value Meaning
lexicon_name 'MALD-1000-test' The words the model knows, and which recordings are used for training (see below)
n_bands 64 Number of frequency bands in the input spectrogram
mechanism, hidden 'LSTM', '192x192x192x192' Four stacked LSTM layers with 192 units each
target_space 'OneHot' One output unit for each word
target_shape 'box' The output unit for a word should be 1 while the word is being said, and 0 otherwise
loss 'dw1024to10' While a word is unfolding, activating other words is penalized 1024 times less. The full penalty applies only during the last 10 frames (100 ms) of each word, and in silence.
stimulus_sequence '2' Training stimuli are a continuous stream of words, with a 200–500 ms pause after every second word on average
snr 20 During training, noise is added to the input at a signal-to-noise ratio of 20 dB
optimizer, learning_rate 'RMSProp', 0.001 Training algorithm
batch_size, steps_per_epoch 32, 25 One epoch consists of 25 batches of 32 ten-second stimuli
seed 0 Random seed for the initial weights

Model name: LSTM-192x192x192x192-dw1024to10-RMSProp-1e-3-32-25-s0 OneHot-box MALD-1000-test-64-2-20 Weights: Models/LSTM-192x192x192x192-dw1024to10-RMSProp-1e-3-32-25-s0 OneHot-box MALD-1000-test-64-2-20/4419.hdf5

The lexicon

The model's lexicon defines which words the model knows and which speakers it has heard. Each combination of a speaker and a word is one token, i.e., one recording. In the MALD-1000-test lexicon, 15 speakers are synthetic text-to-speech voices. The 16th, MALD, is a human speaker (from the Massive Auditory Lexical Decision database), and is the voice that participants heard in the MEG experiment. For the roughly 1000 words that were used in that experiment (called Burgundy in the code), the model was trained on the synthetic voices only – the MALD recordings of those words were held out. This lets us test whether the model can recognize words from a speaker for whom it has never heard those words.

• 2934 words, for example: FRAUGHT, FRAY, FREAK, FREE, FREEDOM, FREEZE, FRENCH, FRESH, FRIEND, FRIENDLY, FRIENDS, FRIENDSHIP, ...
  • 16 speakers: SUSAN, ALEX, TOM, RALPH, VICKI, JUNIOR, AGNES, KATHY, SAMANTHA, BRUCE, VICTORIA, FRED, PRINCESS, AVA, ALLISON, MALD
  • 44010 tokens for training, for example: ('SUSAN', 'BEST')
  • 2934 tokens held out for testing, 998 of which are from the MALD speaker

3. Model input

The model does not hear sound waves directly. Like the human auditory system, it receives a spectrogram: a representation of how much energy the sound contains at different frequencies, and how this changes over time. Specifically, the input is a gammatone spectrogram with 64 frequency bands (from 50 Hz to 10 kHz, spaced like in the cochlea), sampled at 100 Hz – that is, one frame every 10 ms. (The repository's README shows how to create such a spectrogram from a sound file.) lexicon.inputs gives access to the spectrogram for each token, as an array with shape (time, frequency). The files are loaded from disk when they are first needed. Pick a word to see how different speakers say it:

The same word looks quite different depending on who says it: speakers differ in pitch, in speech rate, and in how they pronounce individual sounds. To recognize words, the model has to learn what stays the same across speakers.

4. Creating a stimulus

The model processes continuous speech: there is no signal that tells it where one word ends and the next one begins. We create a stimulus by placing the spectrograms of several words one after another on a timeline. Each word in a stimulus is represented by a Word object, which combines a token (speaker and word) with a time, t0, at which the word starts. Times are counted in frames, so t0=20 means that the word starts 200 ms into the stimulus. Choose the stimulus here (use up to 8 words from the lexicon; the default words are all held-out MALD tokens):

Input and target

gen_input_from_words() turns a sequence of Word objects into arrays. It always generates segments of 1000 frames (10 s), which is the length of stimulus that the network was trained on. For each segment it returns two arrays (the first dimension is for batches, and we only have a single stimulus):
  • The input, with shape (1, time, frequency): silence (zeros) with the spectrogram of each word added at the right time.
  • The target, with shape (1, time, word): what the output of a perfect model would look like. With one-hot targets, each word in the lexicon has its own output unit.
(The same function is used to generate stimuli for training the model, from random sequences of words.)

• inputs: 1000 frames × 64 frequency bands
  • targets: 1000 frames × 2934 words
  • The words end after 369 frames, so we will plot the first 419 frames (4.19 s)

Solid vertical lines mark word onsets, dotted lines mark word offsets. The target for a word is a "box": it is 1 from the onset to the offset of the word. All the other output units (not shown) have a target of 0 throughout. Note that this is an ambitious target: it asks the model to recognize a word from its very first frame. That is impossible, because many words start with the same sounds. How the model deals with this uncertainty is the interesting part.

5. Loading the network

model.load_model() builds the neural network and loads the weights from the last training epoch. Two arguments are worth knowing about:
  • batch_size=1: we want to process one stimulus at a time (training used 32 in parallel).
  • output_hidden=True: the network returns the activity in each hidden layer, in addition to the word outputs.

Reading the summary from top to bottom follows the flow of information: the input (1 stimulus × 1000 frames × 64 frequency bands) passes through four LSTM layers with 192 units each, and a final Dense layer turns the activity of the last LSTM layer into one output for each of the 2934 words. LSTM layers are recurrent: what they do at each frame depends not only on the current input, but also on their own state from the previous frame. This memory is what allows the model to integrate information over the duration of a word.

Training

The model directory also contains a log of the loss during training. The loss measures the mismatch between the model's output and the target, so lower is better.

6. Running the model

model.predict() generates the input for our words (as in section 4), runs it through the network, and collects the results in a dictionary. One detail: the network is stateful. At the end of a 10 s segment it remembers its state, so that a longer stimulus can be processed as a sequence of segments without interruption. Before presenting a new stimulus, we therefore reset the state with network.reset_states().

data contains:
  • 'inputs': array with shape (1000, 64)
  • 'outputs': array with shape (1000, 2934)
  • 'targets': array with shape (1000, 2934)
  • 'hidden0': array with shape (1000, 192)
  • 'hidden1': array with shape (1000, 192)
  • 'hidden2': array with shape (1000, 192)
  • 'hidden3': array with shape (1000, 192)

data.text/markdown:
Word activations

data['outputs'] has the same shape as the target: one value between 0 and 1 for each frame and each word in the lexicon. We can think of this value as the activation of the word – how strongly the model believes that it is hearing this word right now. The figure below shows the input together with the activation of all 2934 words. The words that are actually in the stimulus are drawn in color; all other words are grey. The bottom panel counts how many words are active (activation above 0.5) at each moment.

A few things to notice:
  • Many words become active at word onset. As soon as a word starts, the model activates a whole set of candidate words – typically those that start with similar sounds (the cohort).
  • Competitors drop out as the word unfolds. With every additional sound, fewer candidates are compatible with the input, and the number of active words goes down.
  • Ideally, a single word is left at the end, and it is the one that was actually said.
  • The model is quiet during silence.
This behavior is a consequence of how the model was trained (the loss parameter in section 2): while a word is unfolding, the model is barely penalized for activating other words, so it can afford to keep all plausible candidates active. Only during the last 100 ms of each word does it have to commit.

Competition within each word

To see which words compete, the next figure zooms in on each word of the stimulus. Each panel shows the target word in color, together with the four other words that reached the highest activation while the word was presented. The shaded region marks the last 100 ms of the word, where the training loss applies the full penalty for activating a wrong word.

The competitors usually share their beginning with the target word. Often they stay active until the input contains a sound that rules them out (try PISTOL and PISTON, or CARTON and CARTOON, which only differ late in the word).

Did the model recognize the words?

To decide which word the model "heard", we take the word with the highest activation during the last 100 ms of each word in the stimulus.

data.text/html: 5 of 5 words recognized correctly.

data.text/markdown:
Now go back to section 4 and change the stimulus. For example:
  • Switch to one of the synthetic speakers. Tokens that were used for training are recognized almost perfectly.
  • With the MALD speaker, try some other words from the MEG experiment, for example ATOM BALCONY ASPIRIN. The model has never heard this speaker say these words, and it makes mistakes: it recognizes about 60% of these held-out tokens. When it is wrong, look at the competitors – the errors are often similar-sounding words.
  • Set the silence between words to 0. The model has to find the word boundaries by itself.
  • Set the silence to 50 or 100 ms. During training, words either followed each other directly or were separated by 200–500 ms of silence. Short pauses are something the model has never encountered, and with the MALD speaker it tends to make more mistakes.

7. Hidden layers

So far we have looked at the input and the output of the model. The computations that turn sound into words happen in between, in the four LSTM layers. Because we loaded the network with output_hidden=True, data also contains the activity of each hidden unit: data['hidden0'] (the layer closest to the input) to data['hidden3'] (the layer closest to the output). Each is an array with shape (time, unit), with values between −1 and 1.

Each row is one hidden unit; red is positive and blue is negative activation. In the first layer, activity is moderate and still follows the input fairly closely. Deeper layers use their full range, and their activity looks increasingly different from the spectrogram. The last layer changes abruptly at the end of each word, when the model's output returns to silence.

Summarizing hidden layer activity

To compare a model like this to brain responses, the paper summarizes the activity of each layer with two time series:
  • Magnitude: the sum of the absolute activation of all units in the layer – how active is the layer overall?
  • Onsets: the sum of all increases in absolute activation from one frame to the next – how much new activity appears at each moment?
These time series are then used as predictors for MEG responses to the same stimuli.

Where to go from here

  • Noise: the model was trained with noise in the input. Use model.predict(words=words, model=network, snr=20) to add noise at a signal-to-noise ratio of 20 dB. (To scale the noise, this loads the spectrograms for all training tokens, so it requires the complete GAMMATONE_64_100 directory and takes a moment.)
  • Random stimuli: earshot.train_earshot.gen_words() generates endless random word sequences like the ones used for training.
  • Your own recordings: any spectrogram with 64 gammatone bands at 100 Hz can be used as input – pass it to Word(..., pattern=spectrogram). The README shows how to create one from a sound file.
  • Training a model: after installing the library, the earshot-train command trains a new model; see earshot-train --help for the options, which correspond to the Model parameters in section 2.
